new_statements.quote: Los cuiba-wámonae prefieren no escribir el acento, ya que la posición del acento principal varía. Este generalmente cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra, pero las reglas no son tan sencillas. Para facilitar la lectura de esta gramática de parte de los hispanohablantes, se ha escrito el acento según las reglas de acentuación para el español. Hay solamente unas pocas pares de palabras en las que el acento distingue la una de la otra. Ejemplos: narúntaba ‘quedar’ (‘no ir con otro’) y naruntaba ‘se paró’; taxotsi ‘lo botó para él’ y táxotsi ‘estaba quemado (por el fuego)’. El contexto usualmente las distingue.
new_statements.translation: The Cuiba-Wámonae prefer not to write the accent, since the position of the main accent varies. It generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, but the rules are not so simple. To make this grammar easier for Spanish speakers to read, accent has been written according to the accentuation rules for Spanish. There are only a few pairs of words in which accent distinguishes one from the other. Examples: narúntaba 'to stay' ('not go with another') vs naruntaba 'he/she stood up'; taxotsi 'he threw it away for him' vs táxotsi 'it was burnt (by fire)'. Context usually distinguishes them.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word accent falls by default on the penultimate syllable; the author warns the rules are not simple and a few lexical minimal pairs exist (accent is marginally contrastive). The 2018 dictionary by the same author restates it as 'the accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable; otherwise it is marked', adds that long polymorphemic words have one primary and several secondary accents, and that accent tends to be attracted to diphthong/triphthong syllables, usually the one nearest the end of the word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kerr & Berg 2018, p. 12: 'La palabra larga tiene un solo acento primario y puede tener varios acentos secundarios'; secondary accents are visible on the component morphemes listed under V. (véase) in each entry. Kerr 1995 p. 22 says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: A few minimal pairs (narúntaba/naruntaba, taxotsi/táxotsi; dictionary adds kekoba 'be tight' / kékoba 'rub'); some words vary (wámonae/wamonae); accent attracted to diphthong/triphthong syllables; within a diphthong the first vowel is accented except ua, ue, ui (second), in triphthongs the second except aei, aeu (first) (1995 p. 24; 2018 p. 13).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (la palabra), including long polymorphemic words; citation/dictionary headword forms. Variety: cuiba-wámonae of Mochuelo (Curucutonato tómara), Casanare, Colombia (pin menepiwi sub-dialect; 1995 p. 1).
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources (Kerr 1995; Kerr & Berg 2018) describe the Cuiba-Wámonae of Mochuelo (Curucutonato tómara) on the Casanare river, Colombia (pin menepiwi sub-dialect; Kerr 1995 p. 1 lists sub-dialects pin menepiwi, aitowapiwi/masiguare, wupiwi, siripuxi, mayáraxi, yarawútixi as mutually intelligible). Machal 2000 (Rosetta excerpt) and the Mosonyi works describe the Alto Capanaparo (Venezuela) dialect; Merchán 2000 the Maibén variant. All fall under cuib1242; no dialect-level glottocode assigned here.

new_statements.quote: 3.1.3. El acento. El maibén es una lengua acentual. El ámbito de realización del acento es preferentemente la penúltima sílaba; sin embargo, se encuentran unos cuantos ejemplos en que se acentúa la última sílaba y aun la antepenúltima: dodoupto 'vestido' / pitede 'carbón' / hi'ton 'indígena' / 'wakʌra 'gallina'. Debido a esta posición predecible del acento, en este artículo sólo se marcará cuando no esté en posición canónica. [...] El acento también puede desplazarse al recibir otro morfema: ibo 'piedra' – i'boto 'una piedra'; pen'tonto 'una flor' – penton'ton 'varias flores'. (p. 587) — La ubicación del acento, ya que éste más o menos permite determinar las fronteras de palabra. [...] la palabra es la unidad [...] cuyo acento se da generalmente en la penúltima sílaba. (p. 588)
new_statements.translation: 3.1.3. Accent. Maibén is an accentual language. The domain where accent is realized is preferentially the penultimate syllable; however, a few examples are found in which the last syllable and even the antepenultimate is accented: dodoupto 'dress', pitede 'charcoal', hi'ton 'indigenous person', 'wakʌra 'hen'. Because of this predictable position of the accent, in this article it will be marked only when it is not in canonical position. [...] The accent can also shift when another morpheme is added: ibo 'stone' – i'boto 'a stone'; pen'tonto 'a flower' – penton'ton 'several flowers'. (p. 587) — The location of the accent, since it more or less allows word boundaries to be determined. [...] the word is the unit [...] whose accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable. (p. 588)

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate) and as Kerr 1995; adds that placement is treated as predictable/canonical, names lexical exceptions with final and antepenultimate accent, notes the demarcative function and accent shift under affixation, and describes a specific variant (Maibén of the Resguardo Indígena del Oriente de Casanare, San José del Ariporo) rather than Kerr's Mochuelo dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary accent falls by default on the penultimate syllable of the word; the position is treated as predictable and unmarked, with a few lexical exceptions carrying final or antepenultimate accent (marked in the article). The accent is word-demarcative and re-computes on the derived word when a suffix is added (ibo 'stone' > i'boto), and some segments are reduced to keep the penultimate pattern ('bana > 'banto, 'pona > 'ponhi).
new_statements.exceptions: A few words with final accent (hi'ton 'indígena', pitede 'carbón' as given) or antepenultimate accent ('wakʌra 'gallina', dodoupto 'vestido'); accent shifts under affixation; segment reduction to preserve the accent pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Merchán 2000 describes the Maibén variant of Cuiba spoken in the Resguardo Indígena del Oriente de Casanare (San José del Ariporo), the group the colonos called 'masiwares' (p. 585). Kerr 1995 describes the dialect of the cuiba-wámonae of the pueblo of Mochuelo (Curucutonato tómara), Casanare, i.e. the pin menepiwi originally of the Río Meta, and lists the aitowapiwi/masiguares of San José de Ariporo as a mutually intelligible sub-dialect (IN-1, p. 1 and n. 1). So the two works cover different sub-dialects of cuib1242 and give the same penultimate default.

new_statements.translation: 0-6. Accent. The Cuiba-wámonae prefer not to write the accent, since the position of the main accent varies. It generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, but the rules are not so simple. To make this grammar easier for Spanish speakers to read, the accent has been written according to the Spanish accentuation rules. There are only a few pairs of words in which the accent distinguishes one from the other. Examples: narúntaba 'to stay' ('not go with another') and naruntaba 'he stopped'; taxotsi 'he threw it away for him' and táxotsi 'it was burnt (by fire)'. Context usually distinguishes them. (p. 22) — When a diphthong occurs in an accented syllable, the first vowel of the diphthong bears the accent, except in ua, ue and ui, in which the second bears it. (p. 24)

Adds the diphthong/triphthong accent-position rules of p. 24.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The main accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, but the author says the rules are not simple and does not state them; a few minimal pairs are distinguished by accent alone. Within an accented diphthong the first vowel carries the accent (except ua, ue, ui: second vowel); within an accented triphthong the second vowel (except aei, aeu: the first).
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in sec. 0-6 (the companion Kerr & Berg 2018 dictionary, p. 12, already held by the project, says long words have one primary and several secondary accents)
new_statements.exceptions: 'las reglas no son tan sencillas'; a few minimal pairs contrasting by accent (narúntaba/naruntaba, taxotsi/táxotsi); some dialects lack certain diphthongs/triphthongs (p. 23-24).
new_statements.identity_note: Merchán 2000 describes the Maibén variant of Cuiba spoken in the Resguardo Indígena del Oriente de Casanare (San José del Ariporo), the group the colonos called 'masiwares' (p. 585). Kerr 1995 describes the dialect of the cuiba-wámonae of the pueblo of Mochuelo (Curucutonato tómara), Casanare, i.e. the pin menepiwi originally of the Río Meta, and lists the aitowapiwi/masiguares of San José de Ariporo as a mutually intelligible sub-dialect (IN-1, p. 1 and n. 1). So the two works cover different sub-dialects of cuib1242 and give the same penultimate default.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: both works put the default accent on the penultimate syllable. They differ in emphasis: Merchán (Maibén variant) calls the position 'predecible' and canonical, with only a few lexical exceptions (final or antepenultimate), whereas Kerr (Mochuelo dialect) says the position of the main accent 'varía', that the rules 'no son tan sencillas', and gives minimal pairs distinguished by accent; she therefore writes accent by Spanish conventions rather than stating a rule. Both admit exceptions, so the catalog's 'fixed: penultimate' stands as a default with lexical exceptions rather than an exceptionless rule.
